title: Walking out to greet Shabbat
hookLine: the Safed mystics walk into the fields on Friday to meet Shabbat

cards: Friday, late afternoon, on the edge of Tzfat. The cooking is done, the lamps are ready. And instead of waiting indoors, a group of men walk out of town, down the slope, into the fields.
They face west, toward the setting sun, and begin to sing. They are not going anywhere. They are going out to meet someone.
Tradition says the mystics of Tzfat did this week after week, as if the guest they were greeting were coming up the road.

teach.h: HANINA AND YANNAI GO OUT TO MEET HER.
teach.b: The idea is older than Tzfat. The Talmud tells of two sages and their Friday habits. Rabbi Hanina would wrap himself in his cloak as the sun went down and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen.
Rabbi Yannai would put on his Shabbat clothes and say: come, O bride, come, O bride. Shabbat, in their words, is not just a day that arrives. She is someone you go out to meet.

teach.h: THE MYSTICS WALK INTO THE FIELDS.
teach.b: The mystics of Tzfat took those words literally and walked into the fields. Out of that circle came a poem, Lecha Dodi, written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz.
Its refrain says, in Hebrew, lecha dodi likrat kallah: come, my beloved, to meet the bride. Look closely at the Hebrew: the first letters of its opening verses spell out the poet's name.
The Friday evening psalms that welcome Shabbat in the synagogue, called Kabbalat Shabbat, grew from this same setting, and they lead into the psalm the Bible titles for the day.
It begins: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Today the fields have mostly turned into a doorway.
When the last verse of Lecha Dodi is sung, congregations often turn around to face the synagogue door and bow, as though the bride were walking in. It's a small movement.
But it keeps the old walk alive: Shabbat is still greeted, not just noticed.

how: On Friday evening, Jewish congregations sing Kabbalat Shabbat, including Lecha Dodi, and at its last verse the congregation often turns to face the door to welcome Shabbat as a bride.

practice: If you can, step outside or stand at a window that faces west; if it's not Friday, greet the evening, or simply the next rest you'll have.
Watch the light change on the buildings and the sky, slow and certain, and instead of waiting for rest to find you, turn toward it. If you pray, you can whisper the old words: come, O bride.
